name: Koji-kin (koji mold; kiiro, kuro and shiro types)
text: The Aspergillus mold that makes the enzymes for saccharifying starch and breaking down protein in sake, shochu, awamori, miso and shoyu. Three working types are named by colour: yellow (ki-koji), black (kuro-koji) and white (shiro-koji). They share a genus but differ at the section or species level. Black koji (A. luchuensis) is thought to have been used in Okinawa awamori for a long time; white koji arose as a mutant found in a black-koji culture in the Taisho era.
flavor: Heard first in any koji talk: 'which koji-kin are you running?'
use: 'Sake and miso run yellow koji; awamori runs black; most shochu today runs white.'
craft: Choice of strain is a product decision, not a detail: the acid and enzyme profile of the strain sets what the whole mash can do. Per NRIB, shochu koji makes large amounts of citric acid, so the moromi is strongly acidic, and its enzymes tolerate that pH where yellow-koji enzymes lose activity.
src: Sanwa Shurui koji note: yellow, black, white koji

name: Ki-koji-kin (yellow koji mold)
text: The yellow koji mold, the mainstream strain for sake and also used for miso, shoyu and amazake. It is valued for strong enzyme production while making almost no acid. The fresh, fruity profile commonly attributed to it is a tendency only, since koji alone does not decide flavour.
flavor: Heard in sake, miso and shoyu rooms as the default, unmarked koji.
use: 'It is a standard yellow-koji sake, so acidity comes from the moto, not the koji.'
craft: Because yellow koji makes little acid, acid control in sake falls to the shubo (lactic acid) rather than the koji. Its enzymes lose activity in the strongly acidic mash typical of shochu, which is one reason shochu uses citric-acid-producing strains.
src: Nomooo: black, white and yellow koji

name: Kuro-koji-kin (black koji mold)
text: The black koji mold (Aspergillus luchuensis), associated with awamori in Okinawa and with shochu in hot, humid Kagoshima. It produces abundant citric acid, which suppresses spoilage bacteria. Its traditional drawback was that spores drift and blacken equipment and work clothes. It is said to give body and umami, but that is a tendency, not a rule.
flavor: Heard in awamori and Kagoshima shochu, 'kuro' on the label means heavier, richer.
use: 'This is a black-koji awamori, made with all-koji mash.'
craft: The citric acid is what makes it practical in warm climates. Black spore dust is the housekeeping problem; this is why white koji, a mutant of black, took over much of shochu making.
src: Denen Shuzo: black koji and Kagoshima shochu

name: Shiro-koji-kin (white koji mold)
text: The white koji mold, found as a spontaneous mutant during black-koji culture in the Taisho era. Like black koji it produces a lot of citric acid, which holds back contaminating bacteria, but it is cleaner to handle because it does not stain. It is now the mainstream shochu koji. Some sake makers use it deliberately to add a fresh acidity.
flavor: Heard on shochu labels as 'shiro-koji', meaning lighter and milder than black.
use: 'The imo shochu is a white-koji product, light and easy to work with.'
craft: Do not confuse shiro-koji (the white mold strain) with 'shio-koji' (salt koji seasoning) or with plain rice koji, which is made with yellow koji and also looks white when grown.

name: Tane-koji (seed koji, koji spores)
text: Koji-mold spores prepared for seeding steamed rice. In koji making the spores are sprinkled over cooled steamed rice at the tanekiri step and worked in by hand. The strain bought or used (yellow for sake, black or white for shochu and awamori) fixes the character of the koji that grows.
flavor: Heard in the koji room when talking about which strain went on the rice.
use: 'We switched the tane-koji for the ginjo lot.'
craft: Strain selection is made before the rice is touched. This entry does not cover spore counts, dosage rates or supplier specifics; those were not in the sources reviewed and should be taken from the maker's own spec sheet.

name: Seikiku (koji making, koji-zukuri)
text: The process of growing koji mold on steamed rice in the koji-muro, a hot, humid room. The steps are hikikomi, tanekiri, tokomomi, kirikaeshi, mori, nakashigoto, shimai-shigoto and dekoji. Sources describe a total of roughly 48 hours. The finished koji is taken out at about 40-43 C and then cooled and dried (karashi).
flavor: Heard in every sake kura: the koji process decides the quality of the brew.
use: 'Seikiku starts at hikikomi in the afternoon and the koji is out two days later.'
craft: The whole job is managing temperature and moisture of the rice mass, using the hand-work steps below. A koji-buta (tray) or box holds the rice in small lots after mori to stop the centre overheating.
src: Kurabito: how koji is made, with temperature control

name: Tanekiri and tokomomi (seeding and bed-mixing)
text: After the steamed rice is brought into the koji room (hikikomi), spores are sprinkled over it (tanekiri) and rubbed through by hand (tokomomi) so that every grain is inoculated. Some kura repeat the tanekiri and tokomomi pair several times.
flavor: Heard as the first hands-on moment of the koji room.
use: 'Do the tokomomi gently; the rice is still cooling.'
craft: The aim is even inoculation. Uneven seeding means uneven growth, and the later kirikaeshi and mori can only correct the temperature and moisture, not the spore distribution.
src: Sake-kagiya: traditional hand koji making (Kobayashi Shuzo)

name: Kirikaeshi and mori (turning and dividing)
text: Kirikaeshi is the first turn, done when mold growth begins and the rice temperature climbs, sources give about 36 C. It loosens clumped grains and evens out temperature and moisture. Mori follows at about 35 C: the rice is divided into koji-buta (trays) or boxes so the centre does not overheat. At mori, hase (mycelial spots) should be visible as dots.
flavor: Heard as the cue that the koji has started to take off.
use: 'Temperature is 36, time for kirikaeshi.'
craft: Timing is by rice temperature and feel, not by clock. The point of splitting into trays at mori is purely thermal: a single large mass cannot shed the heat the growing mold makes.

name: Nakashigoto, shimai-shigoto and dekoji (finishing the koji)
ja: 仲仕事・仕舞仕事・出麹
text: Nakashigoto is done when the temperature is 34-36 C: the koji is mixed to release moisture and supply oxygen. Shimai-shigoto is the last handling, drawing finger lines through the koji to shed heat and encourage evaporation. Dekoji is taking the finished koji out of the room, held at about 40-43 C, after which it is cooled and dried (karashi).
flavor: Heard in the second day of koji making.
use: 'Nakashigoto at four, shimai at noon, dekoji by evening.'
craft: These steps steer how hard the koji is driven. Moisture release is the lever: more drying holds back the mold. The exact hours are the kura's own and vary with rice and style.

name: Moromi (fermenting mash)
text: The soft, partly solid mash of a brew in progress. In sake, moromi is the tank contents after koji, steamed rice and water have been added to the moto. In shoyu, moromi is steamed soybeans and roasted, cracked wheat made into koji, then mixed with brine; pressing it gives liquid shoyu and a solid cake. The kanji 醪 and 諸味 are both used.
flavor: Heard across sake, shoyu and shochu making.
use: 'The moromi is on day twelve and still bubbling.'
craft: Do not mix up the stages: 'moromi' is the pre-press mash in every trade, while the pressed leftover is kasu (sake) or shoyu cake. The shochu primary and secondary mashes are called ichiji and niji moromi.

name: Shubo / moto (yeast starter)
text: The yeast starter in sake making, grown in quantity before the main mash. Shochu has the same idea in its first mash (ichiji moromi), described as the equivalent of the sake shubo: yeast is multiplied so that the main mash ferments safely. The sake types of moto are kimoto, yamahai, sokujo, bodaimoto.
flavor: Heard when asking how the mash was started.
use: 'Which moto is it, kimoto or sokujo?'
craft: The moto is where acid is set in sake. Choice of moto (see kimoto, yamahai, sokujo, bodaimoto) is the main reason two sakes of the same rice and polish can differ in acidity and body.

name: Kimoto (traditional starter with yamaoroshi)
text: The most traditional moto: lactic acid comes from naturally occurring lactic bacteria, and the rice, koji and water are ground in the yamaoroshi step. Sources give roughly one month to bring the moto up, against about 15 days for sokujo. Kikumasamune publishes research on the ethanol tolerance of kimoto yeasts.
flavor: Heard on labels for a fuller, more acidic style.
use: 'Kimoto-zukuri, so expect lactic acidity and depth.'
craft: Commonly confused with yamahai, which omits the yamaoroshi. Kimoto gives more acid and body but the sources stress that this is a tendency, with big variation by brewery.
src: Sawanotsuru: what is kimoto, and the difference from yamahai
Kikumasamune: kimoto yeast ethanol tolerance study

name: Yamahai (kimoto without yamaoroshi)
text: A moto that, like kimoto, adds no lactic acid and relies on lactic bacteria living in the kura, but skips the yamaoroshi grinding. Sources give about four weeks for the moto stage. Because it removes a heavy manual job it was a labour-saving step relative to kimoto.
flavor: Heard on labels as 'yamahai-jikomi'.
use: 'Yamahai, so no added lactic acid and no yamaoroshi.'
craft: The practical line between yamahai and kimoto is the yamaoroshi step alone. Both are acid-forward and slow versus sokujo; period figures vary between sources (about four weeks, 30-40 days).
src: Sake Times: five questions about kimoto and yamahai (Tamba toji)

name: Sokujo-moto (quick-fermentation starter)
text: The moto made by adding brewers' lactic acid at the start rather than waiting for lactic bacteria to grow. Sources give about 15 days for the moto stage, against about 30 for kimoto-types, and describe it as the mainstream method, one source puts it at roughly 90 percent of sake.
flavor: Heard as the unmarked default; labels rarely say it.
use: 'It is a sokujo, so the moto was ready in a couple of weeks.'
craft: The sources associate sokujo with a clean, clear profile, but this is a tendency, not a guarantee. The speed and safety of the added acid is why it spread.
src: Sakesen: differences between kimoto, yamahai, sokujo

name: Bodaimoto (Shoryakuji starter, soyashi-mizu)
text: A starter said to have been developed at Shoryakuji temple in Nara in the mid-Muromachi period. Its feature is soyashi-mizu: acidic water made by lactic fermentation of raw rice soaked in water, with a yogurt-like sourness, used as the brewing water. Today Shoryakuji adds its own lactic acid bacteria (Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis), found in spring water in the temple hills; research notes say steamed rice for the soyashi can then be omitted.
flavor: Heard in talk of the oldest, 'origin' style of sake.
use: 'The bodaimoto-zukuri sake uses soyashi-mizu in place of plain water.'
craft: Sources differ on soaking time (about two to three days). Distinguish it from mizumoto, which the same sources describe as a related lactic-water method developed independently by individual kura.
src: Sake Times: Bodaimoto festival at Shoryakuji

name: Sandan-shikomi (three-stage mash building)
text: The standard sake mash method: the moto goes in the tank, and koji, steamed rice and water are added in three portions rather than at once. Some kura use four or even ten stages. Staging keeps the yeast population from being overwhelmed and lets the mash build up.
flavor: Heard when explaining how sake mash is built.
use: 'Standard sandan-shikomi, over four days.'
craft: Step sizes and intervals are a kura's own recipe. This entry does not give the traditional stage names or ratios since the sources reviewed did not state them.
src: Sakeworld: parallel multiple fermentation and three-stage mashing

name: Heiko fukuhakko (parallel multiple fermentation)
text: The characteristic of sake fermentation in which koji enzymes turning starch into sugar and yeast turning sugar into alcohol run at the same time in the same tank. It is contrasted with wine, which has single fermentation of sugar already in the fruit.
flavor: Heard in technical explanations of why sake can reach high alcohol.
use: 'Sake is heiko fukuhakko; the sugar is made and eaten at once.'
craft: Because saccharification and fermentation overlap, mash temperature management has to serve both enzymes and yeast; this is the core reason sake mash is held cold and staged.

name: Seimai-buai (rice polishing ratio)
text: The weight of polished rice as a percentage of the brown rice. Under the NTA standard, fractions under 1 percent are truncated, so 69.8 percent is written as 69 percent. Polishing ratio is a labeling standard for the special designation sakes. The label standard was set in 1989 and applied from April 1990; a 2004 revision made the ratio mandatory for all special-designation sakes, per Gekkeikan's description.
flavor: Heard as a number on the label: 50, 60, 70.
use: 'Seimai-buai 40 percent: sixty percent of the grain was milled away.'
craft: A lower number means more removed, not more rice. Because of the truncation rule, the stated figure is the ceiling, not the exact value.

name: Shinpaku (white core of sake rice)
text: The opaque white centre of a sake-rice grain, made of starch. Koji mold hyphae enter the gaps there, one reason it is sought after in sake rice. Yamada Nishiki, bred in Hyogo, is large and has shinpaku.
flavor: Heard in discussions of sake-rice quality.
use: 'Good shinpaku, and a big grain, so it takes high polish.'
craft: A common misunderstanding is that shinpaku equals quality in itself. It matters for koji growth; sources address misconceptions and ongoing research, but the details are not summarized here.
src: Science Museum: sake and science (Yamada Nishiki grain)

name: Kojimai and kakemai (koji rice and mash rice)
text: Kojimai is white rice used to make koji; kakemai is the rest of the rice, steamed and added directly to the moromi. Kakemai is the bulk of the rice, one source says about 70 percent of the total.
flavor: Heard in recipes and brewing logs.
use: 'Kojimai is Yamada Nishiki, kakemai is a table-rice grade.'
craft: Makers can use different varieties or polishing for the two. The sources do not give polishing figures for each, so check against the label and the kura's own spec.

name: Tokutei meisho-shu (special-designation sake)
text: Sake that may carry designated names (junmai, ginjo, daiginjo, honjozo and combinations) under the NTA's sake labeling standard (Heisei 1 NTA Notice No.8, set 1989). The names are defined by polishing ratio, use of brewers' alcohol and, for ginjo types, ginjo-style brewing.
flavor: Heard on every premium bottle.
use: 'It is a tokutei meisho-shu, junmai ginjo at 55 percent.'
craft: Sources disagree on the date of a revision that dropped the old 70 percent polishing requirement for junmai-shu; the Nissyoku article does not state the year clearly. Check the current NTA notice for exact conditions.

name: Ginjo and daiginjo (ginjo-zukuri grades)
text: Under the NTA standard, ginjo uses white rice polished to 60 percent or less and ginjo-style brewing, with good flavour and colour. Daiginjo uses 50 percent or less, with especially good flavour and colour. Junmai ginjo and junmai daiginjo are the same grades without brewers' alcohol.
flavor: Heard as the premium tier.
use: 'Daiginjo, 40 percent: a polished, aromatic style.'
craft: The thresholds are ceilings; many daiginjo are polished far below 50. The 'junmai' prefix is only about alcohol; the polish ratio rules are as for the base grade.

name: Junmai-shu (pure rice sake)
text: A designation for sake made without added brewers' alcohol. The NTA outline gives no polishing-ratio requirement for plain junmai. Junmai daiginjo is a daiginjo polishing grade (50 percent or less) made without brewers' alcohol.
flavor: Heard on labels as a mark of rice-only sake.
use: 'Junmai, no alcohol added, and polished to 60.'
craft: 'Junmai' says nothing about polishing by itself; check seimai-buai on the label separately. Older descriptions that cite a 70 percent condition for junmai are out of date per the sources, though the revision year was not confirmed.

name: Honjozo-shu (sake with added brewers' alcohol)
text: A designation for sake made from white rice polished to 70 percent or less, with brewers' alcohol added. It is the entry point of the special-designation sakes.
flavor: Heard as the everyday premium tier.
use: 'Honjozo at 65 percent, light and dry.'
craft: The added alcohol is a brewing step, not a defect. Tied to the polish ratio ceiling of 70 percent, as per the NTA notice.

name: Nama-zake, namachozo and namazume (unheated sakes)
ja: 生酒・生貯蔵酒・生詰め酒
text: Sake is normally heated (hiire) twice, before storage and before shipping. Nama-zake is never heated. Namachozo is not heated before storage but is heated once before shipping. Namazume is heated before storage and not heated at shipping. Nama-genshu is unheated and undiluted.
flavor: Heard on seasonal and fresh-style bottles.
use: 'Namazake needs cold storage; namazume is more forgiving.'
craft: Deterioration smells differ: heated sake kept warm gets 'hineka' (aged smell), unheated sake kept at room temperature gets 'mureka'.

name: Genshu (undiluted sake)
text: Sake that has not been diluted with water after pressing. It says nothing about heating: genshu may or may not have been pasteurised, and it is a separate axis from nama.
flavor: Heard on labels for stronger, fuller bottles.
use: 'Genshu, so it is bottled straight from the press at full strength.'
craft: The classic mix-up is nama versus genshu. Nama means unheated; genshu means undiluted; a nama-genshu is both.

name: Hiire (pasteurisation by heating)
text: Heating sake to sterilise it and stabilise quality. Normally done twice, before storage and before shipping. Which of the two heatings is skipped defines nama-zake, namachozo and namazume.
flavor: Heard when a bottle is described as heated or unheated.
use: 'Hiire was done once, before tank storage.'
craft: Spoilage smells are named by history: 'hineka' from heated sake kept warm, 'mureka' from unheated sake at room temperature. Exact heating temperatures were not in the sources reviewed.

name: Toji (master brewer)
text: The person with top responsibility for making the sake, one per kura. Under the toji, the kashira (deputy) directs work and staffing; the daishi runs koji making; the motomawari or motoya runs the moto. Traditionally toji came as seasonal migrant teams from farm villages, such as the Nanbu toji (Iwate, 600+ members in 2020) and Tamba toji (Hyogo, around 18 per kura).
flavor: Heard when asking who made the sake.
use: 'The toji runs the kura from the koji room to the press.'
craft: The toji and the kuramoto (owner) are different roles. A kuramoto-toji is an owner who also brews. Team sizes and numbers vary by source.

name: Kuramoto and kurabito (brewery owner and brewing staff)
text: The kuramoto runs the whole brewery as a business. Kurabito are the brewing workers under the toji. Traditionally the kuramoto left brewing to migrant toji and kurabito, though kuramoto-toji, owners who brew themselves, have become more common.
flavor: Heard when distinguishing business from craft.
use: 'The kuramoto owns the label; the kurabito make the sake.'
craft: Do not use kuramoto for the maker as a person; it is the proprietor. Whether a company's staff are seasonal or full-time varies by brewery.

name: Ichiji-shikomi and niji-shikomi (shochu two-stage mashing)
ja: 一次仕込み・二次仕込み
text: Shochu is made in two stages. The primary mash (ichiji) grows yeast from koji, water and yeast, and corresponds to the sake shubo. The secondary mash (niji) adds the main ingredient (potato, barley, etc.) to the primary moromi for saccharification and fermentation. The method is said to have been established in Kagoshima around 1914. Citric acid from the koji suppresses bacteria in the warm Kyushu climate.
flavor: Heard in shochu distillery tours.
use: 'Ichiji moromi on day five, then the sweet potato goes in for niji.'
craft: The primary mash is about yeast safety, not flavour; the main ingredient defines the character at the secondary stage.
src: Honkaku Shochu and Awamori: how shochu is made
Chiba Sake: how shochu is made

name: Zen-koji shikomi (all-koji mash for awamori)
text: The awamori method: all the raw material is made into rice koji and mashed once with water and yeast, instead of the two-stage shochu method. One reason given is that a two-stage mash spoils more easily in hot, humid Okinawa.
flavor: Heard on awamori tours and labels.
use: 'Awamori is zen-koji; there is no second mash.'
craft: Black koji and its citric acid are what make a single, all-koji mash safe. Awamori is also distilled at atmospheric pressure.
src: Honkaku Shochu and Awamori: how shochu is made
Chiba Sake: how shochu is made

name: Kusu / koshu and shitsugi (aged awamori)
text: Under the awamori fair-competition code revised 10 Oct 2013 and applied from 1 Aug 2015, 'kusu' may be labeled only if the entire content has been stored three years or more. Before, over 50 percent was enough. Blended kusu are labeled with the youngest age. Shitsugi is topping up old awamori with slightly younger awamori to prevent deterioration. An industry guideline from 2021 treats spirits over 45 percent the same way.
flavor: Heard in awamori shops and on labels.
use: 'A 10-year kusu; the shitsugi cask is in the back.'
craft: Some articles still quote the old over-50-percent rule; those are outdated.

name: Joatsu and genatsu jochu (atmospheric and reduced-pressure distillation)
text: Atmospheric distillation heats at normal pressure, leaving more heat-formed flavour compounds and typically a robust profile. Reduced-pressure distillation lowers the pot pressure so it boils at about 40-50 C, giving less heat-derived aroma and a typically cleaner profile. Awamori is characterized by atmospheric distillation.
flavor: Heard when comparing shochu styles.
use: 'Joatsu for the heavier imo; genatsu for the light barley.'
craft: The rule 'joatsu = heavy, genatsu = clean' is a tendency only; one distiller's interview challenges that simple split. Taste the product, not the method.
src: Shochu Next: Nishi Shuzo on distillation

name: Tennen jozo (naturally brewed, JAS term)
text: A label term for shoyu and similar products. Per JAS, it may be used only when the product is honjozo-made, no enzymes or other process-accelerating treatments are used, and no food additives are used.
flavor: Heard on shoyu labels.
use: 'The label says tennen jozo, so no accelerants.'
craft: It states a method, not a quality grade or maturation time. Check the three JAS conditions rather than inferring a long ferment.

name: Hon-mirin (true mirin)
text: A seasoning made from glutinous rice, rice koji and shochu, saccharified and aged for about two months. It is distinct from 'mirin-fu chomiryo' (mirin-style seasoning).
flavor: Heard in kitchens and on labels.
use: 'Use hon-mirin, not mirin-fu seasoning, for the glaze.'
craft: Check the ingredient list: rice, rice koji and shochu mean hon-mirin. Other details of the process were not in the sources reviewed.
src: Chikyujin Club: fermented seasonings, real versus imitation
